title: This Is God's House, the Gate of Heaven — Stone, Stairway, Oil
blocks: Peace to you, brothers and sisters. The last lesson left us with two brothers — one who cried out with a great and bitter cry, and one who had to run for his life that same night. Their mother said, "Stay a few days." It turned out to be twenty years.
Today's lesson walks out of the front door together with the one who is running. And before we take a step further, I want to put a question to you.

If God were going to appear to a person, which day do you suppose he would pick? Presumably the day that person is at his most devout and his cleanest — the day he has just finished confessing his sins, the day his heart is at its softest.

But in Genesis chapter 28, the night God appeared to Jacob was the first night of his flight: he had just finished deceiving his blind father, his brother had sworn to kill him, and he was running through the dark. All he had in his hand was a staff, and when he lay down to sleep he took a stone for a pillow.

Let me put the answer up front. The night God appeared to Jacob was the least deserving night of his whole life. God did not wait for the man to improve before he came, and he did not say one word of rebuke — first he takes hold of you, and afterwards he deals with you.
1. On a Refugee's Travel Papers, the Seal of the Promise
In verses 1 to 5, Isaac sends Jacob away to Paddan-aram, and the reason he gives is this: you shall not take a wife of the daughters of Canaan.

Brothers and sisters, that is the public version of the matter. The truth is in chapter 27, verses 42 and 43, where Rebekah says, "Behold, your brother Esau comforts himself about you by planning to kill you. Now therefore, my son, obey my voice. Arise, flee to Laban, my brother, in Haran."
What the family said was: go and find a wife. What was actually happening was: run for your life.

But look carefully at verses 3 and 4, at what Isaac says as he sends him off: "May God Almighty bless you, and make you fruitful, and multiply you … and give you the blessing of Abraham, to you and to your offspring with you."

"God Almighty" is אֵל שַׁדַּי (*El Shaddai*) — the very name by which God revealed himself to Abraham in Genesis 17:1. And here, in this sending-off, Isaac formally hands the covenant of Abraham on to Jacob.
Brothers and sisters, do you see the combination? A refugee's travel papers — and stamped across them, the seal of the promise.

And this is intensely practical for us. Some of the roads in a life are roads you are forced to walk: being made redundant, being frozen out, being driven away from a place you wanted to stay in, being pushed along by a diagnosis you never asked for. And this chapter tells you that one and the same forced road can be carrying a promise at the same time. The road you are walking at this moment, the one you did not choose for yourself — that does not mean God has not sent you down it.
Verses 6 to 9 hold a little episode that usually gets skipped over: Esau saw that the daughters of Canaan did not please his father, so off he went and married a daughter of Ishmael.

Brothers and sisters, he was trying very hard to get it right. But the branch he went to was Ishmael's — the line that had been sent away eastward, the line outside the promise. He wanted to correct his course, and he corrected it onto a side branch.

And in these few verses the text has Esau seeing three times — he saw that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him away, he saw that Jacob had obeyed and gone, he saw that the daughters of Canaan did not please his father — while for Jacob it uses one verb: he obeyed. Jacob was listening; Esau was looking. There are people who spend a whole lifetime working very hard at pleasing somebody, and never once go back to their father and ask the one question: what would you have me do?
Jacob is on the run. Why would God appear at a moment like that, and hand him a promise on top of it?

This is the most startling thing in the whole chapter. He had just finished deceiving his father, his brother had just sworn to kill him, and he was heading north alone. The text says he "came to a certain place, and stayed there all night, because the sun had set. He took one of the stones of the place, and put it under his head" — a night with nothing in it at all. And God appears there, and in everything he says there is not one word of rebuke; it is promise from beginning to end. This is not indulgence. It is the order in which grace works: God first gives a person somewhere to stand, and only then, slowly, deals with what is wrong with him — and that took twenty years. So if you are sitting in the middle of a mess you made yourself, this chapter is telling you: God does not wait until you have cleared it up before he is willing to show up.
Is the promise God gives Jacob the same as the one he gave Abraham?

The content is the same — the land, the offspring, all the families of the earth blessed in him. It is one and the same covenant, now handed down to the third generation. But this chapter adds something intensely personal: "Behold, I am with you, and will keep you, wherever you go, and will bring you again into this land. For I will not leave you until I have done that which I have spoken of to you." Which is to say: alongside the promise made to a people, God gave him a guarantee made to a person. And that is very practical for us. A great promise of God only becomes warm when it lands on one particular human being. So when you are reading a promise, add one more question to your reading: in this passage, which sentence is God saying to me, personally, right now?
2. A Light from the Original: a Stairway Set Upon the Earth

Verses 10 and 11: "Jacob went out from Beersheba, and went toward Haran. He came to a certain place, and stayed there all night, because the sun had set. He took one of the stones of the place, and put it under his head, and lay down in that place to sleep."
Brothers and sisters, picture that night for a moment. His first day away from home; the light gone; no tent, no servants, nothing but a staff. He takes a stone and puts it under his head.
And the text goes out of its way to say "because the sun had set" — he had not planned to spend the night there. He walked until he could not walk any further.
Then verse 12: "He dreamed and saw a stairway set upon the earth, and its top reached to heaven. Behold, the angels of God were ascending and descending on it."

The word behind "stairway" is סֻלָּם (*sulam*), and in the whole of the Old Testament it occurs exactly once — here. It can mean a ladder; it can equally mean a ramp or a flight of steps. And most scholars point out that what it describes looks very like a Mesopotamian ziggurat — the sort of stepped platform that stood behind the tower of Babel in chapter 11.
Brothers and sisters, there is a very important comparison to be made here.
In chapter 11, human beings built a tower whose "top reaches to the sky" — and the building stopped, and the name of the place was rewritten as "confusion."
In chapter 28, God lets down a stairway, its "top reached to heaven" — and it stands.

The tower human beings built to reach heaven failed; the stairway God let down succeeded. And notice which way the angels are moving: "ascending and descending." Up first, and then down. Which is to say, they were already here — it was Jacob who did not know it.
Verse 13: "Behold, Yahweh stood above it, and said, 'I am Yahweh, the God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac.'"

And then come four sentences beginning "I will": "I will give the land you lie on to you and to your offspring … Behold, I am with you, and will keep you, wherever you go, and will bring you again into this land. For I will not leave you until I have done that which I have spoken of to you."
Brothers and sisters, count the sentences of rebuke in that speech.

He had just deceived his father, cheated his brother out of the blessing, and put God's own name inside a lie. And the first thing God says is "I am Yahweh" — and after that it is nothing but promise.

The discipline will come — over the next twenty years, not one stroke of it is spared him. But what God gives first is an identity, not a rebuke. He always settles you in the certainty that he is still there, and only then does he start pruning.
What exactly was that stairway? Does it have anything to do with the Lord Jesus?

The Hebrew סֻלָּם (*sulam*) occurs only this once in the whole Old Testament, and its sense is close to "ramp" or "flight of steps"; some scholars think the picture is close to the stairway of an ancient Mesopotamian ziggurat. But the interpretation that matters most is the one the Lord Jesus gave himself. In John 1:51 he says to Nathanael, "you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man." He takes that stairway and points it at himself. So the heart of this passage is not "a person can climb up" — nobody climbs that stairway — but that between heaven and earth there is a road God has opened, and that road was later given a name.
"Set upon the earth, and its top reached to heaven" — is there something in that direction?

The last time human beings tried to join heaven and earth was the tower of Babel in chapter 11: people building from the bottom upwards, and the result was that they were scattered. This time God lets something down from the top, and the stairway is set on the earth first. The same joining of heaven and earth — one made by people, one given by God. That contrast is very nearly the whole Bible in miniature: religion is people climbing up, the gospel is God walking down. And it is worth noticing where this happened — on a night when a fugitive and a deceiver was lying out in the open with a stone under his head. The place God put the stairway down was not a temple; it was the wilderness. So the question we have to ask is not "how do I get up there?" It is "do I recognise that he has already come down?"
3. Surely Yahweh Is in This Place, and I Didn't Know It
Verse 16: "Jacob awakened out of his sleep, and he said, 'Surely Yahweh is in this place, and I didn't know it.'"
Brothers and sisters, that sentence is worth stopping over for a long while.
What changed was not where God was. What changed was his eyes.
That place had no altar, no temple, no priest, no history of worship. It had one stone doing duty as a pillow, and one man on the run. And God was there.
Verse 17: "He was afraid, and said, 'How awesome this place is! This is none other than God's house, and this is the gate of heaven.'"
"God's house" is בֵּית־אֵל (*Beit-El*) — Bethel. "The gate of heaven" is שַׁעַר הַשָּׁמָיִם.
Brothers and sisters, there was not a building of any description in that place. He calls it God's house because God was there.

So please do not tie your faith to a location. Verse 16 puts it plainly enough: God was already there, and the man simply did not know it. And Acts 7:48 says, "the Most High doesn't dwell in temples made with hands."
Verse 18: "Jacob rose up early in the morning, and took the stone that he had put under his head, and set it up for a pillar, and poured oil on its top."
Somebody will ask: setting up a pillar and pouring oil over it — is that not a pagan practice? Does Deuteronomy 16:22 not forbid setting up pillars?

Brothers and sisters, mind the sequence. The law is still hundreds of years away from being given. And the purpose of his pillar is to be a marker, a memorial that God appeared in this place — not an image to be worshipped. Straight afterwards he names the place, and he makes a vow. What the law would later forbid is treating the pillar as the object of worship. You may have markers. There is only one who may be the object.
"Surely Yahweh is in this place, and I didn't know it" — why did he not know?

Because he assumed God was in certain places and on certain people: in his father's tent, in the ceremony of blessing, in that family atmosphere where God was said to be present. It had never occurred to him that God was also out on the road with a man running away. And the next thing he says — "How awesome this place is!" — uses the word for holy fear. That is a very practical warning to us. We are forever tying God down to particular settings: church, meetings, songs, the spiritual high points. And the result is that in exactly the places where we need him most — a hospital corridor, the small hours of a night of overtime, the silence after a quarrel — we assume he is not there. In practice you can make an exercise of it: every day, in one place that does not feel as though God is in it, say one sentence — "Lord, you are here too."

Verses 20 to 22: "Jacob vowed a vow, saying, 'If God will be with me, and will keep me in this way that I go, and will give me bread to eat, and clothing to put on, so that I come again to my father's house in peace, and Yahweh will be my God.'"
Brothers and sisters, that prayer grates a little when you read it, doesn't it?
God said "I will" four times. He answered with one "if."

And he shrinks God's promise down as well. What God said was, "I will give the land you lie on to you and to your offspring", and, "In you and in your offspring, all the families of the earth will be blessed." What he asks for is food, clothing, and a safe journey home.
From a promise of that size, down to something to eat, something to wear, and getting home in one piece.
But brothers and sisters, I want you to notice two things.

First: every single item he asks for, God had already promised him in verse 15. So this is not a negotiation. This is somebody who has only just learned to pray, reading the words back — taking what he has heard and saying it again in his own words. That is not irreverence. That is what a beginner looks like.
Second, and this is the important one: he says a sentence he has never said before in his life — "Yahweh will be my God."
Go back to chapter 27, verse 20. What he said to his father there was "Yahweh your God."
And now he says, "Yahweh will be my God."
It is a very rough starting point. But it is a starting point.

Brothers and sisters, do not look down on how self-interested a new believer's prayers sound. Jacob's first prayer asked for something to eat, something to wear, and a safe journey home. God did not look down on it. God took twenty years to bring him to the ford of the Jabbok, and there at last he got the truth out of his own mouth — asked his name, he answered, "Jacob."
God caught that "if" — and he did not leave him standing there.
Jacob says, "If God will be with me … and Yahweh will be my God." Is it all right to drive a bargain with God like that?

The text records it exactly as it was and does not tidy it up for him. And what is worth noticing is God's reaction: he did not withdraw the promise, and he did not rebuke him. Two things have to be said here together. First, this is an immature faith — his "if" is haggling with God; that was the height he stood at then, and Scripture honestly leaves it standing. Second, God caught that "if", and twenty years later, in chapter 31, he says to him in person, "I am the God of Bethel." So we can put it like this: God allows a person to begin from an immature place, but he will not let a person stay there. If your prayers today are still very self-interested, there is no need to pretend otherwise. Say them out loud, and let God take his time growing you up.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is preaching the stairway to heaven as something a person can climb by trying hard. People draw it out as a "ladder of spiritual growth", one rung at a time, all the way up. But the text says the angels were "ascending and descending", and the stairway was set there by God; and in John 1:51 the Lord Jesus says, "you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man." He replaces the stairway with himself. Preach it as a ladder of achievement, and your congregation walks straight back into religion.

The second is preaching Jacob's vow as a model of faith. God said "I will" four times; he answered with one "if", and shrank the promise down to food, clothing and getting home safely. Teach that as a model, and what your congregation learns is a faith that drives bargains. What has to be preached is this: God caught that "if" — and that is grace, not the quality of his faith.

The third is using "Bethel" to argue that some particular location carries a special power of God. Verse 16 says God was already there and the man simply did not know it. The location is not what matters. Preach it as a holy site, and your congregation will tie their faith to premises, and then start chasing conferences and chasing places.

The fourth is preaching the grace and never preaching the twenty years that came afterwards. God caught that "if" — and then took twenty years to bring him from Jacob to Israel. Preach acceptance on its own, and your congregation will assume grace does not bring change. Grace is free. It has never once been static.

The fifth is skipping the paragraph about Esau marrying a daughter of Ishmael. Those verses look like an aside; in fact they are the control group for the whole chapter. One man is found by God in a dream; the other is working hard at pleasing his father. And the text uses two verbs — "saw" and "obeyed" — to separate the two kinds of life.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: I have done something very serious, and I feel I have no face left to pray with — should I get it "cleared up" first and then come back to God? Brothers and sisters, the answer this chapter gives is perfectly clear: you do not have to, and you could not if you tried. That night was the least deserving night of Jacob's whole life, and God appeared on that night, with not one word of rebuke. This matters particularly among Chinese people, because our culture is thoroughly at home with the rule that you tidy yourself up before you go and see anybody — change your clothes before you call on an elder, work out your explanation before you own up to trouble. But the prodigal son in Luke 15 was still a long way off when the father ran to him and fell on his neck, and he was never even allowed to finish the speech he had prepared. So pray tonight, and come as you are. As for the thing that has to be dealt with — God will work through it with you over the next twenty years, one item at a time. He really will deal with it, but that comes after the relationship is restored, not before.

The second question: Chinese people take feng shui, the energy of a place, temples and the ancestral house very seriously, and feel that certain places are especially potent. Is Bethel a place of that kind? Brothers and sisters, this chapter turns that mindset exactly the other way round. Verse 16 says, "Surely Yahweh is in this place, and I didn't know it" — it was not that the ground was special to begin with; it was that God spoke to him there that night. And notice: it was not a temple. It was open wasteland, and he only slept there because he had walked until he could walk no further. So how might a Christian talk about this with the elders of the family? You could say: you are right, a person does need a marker, a place he can go back to. What I came to find out is that the marker is not a patch of ground looking after me; it is that I met there a God who comes along with me — in verse 15 he says, "I am with you, and will keep you, wherever you go." That is the biggest difference of all: ground does not move, and he walks with you.
We say "God's presence is here" all the time. How do we keep that from turning into a cult of feelings?

Three practical tests. First, the ground of the presence is God's word, not the atmosphere: what Jacob had to go on in this chapter was the few sentences God spoke, not the emotion of the moment. Second, the proof of the presence is in the life that comes afterwards: in chapter 31 God says, "I am the God of Bethel" — something still standing twenty years later. Third, presence does not mean things go smoothly: what comes next for him is being cheated over a marriage, having his wages changed ten times, and running away twice. So in judging whether God is there or not, do not go by today's feelings. Go by what he has said, and by whether he is still there wherever you have got to. Feelings are a gift. They are not a measuring instrument.
7. Living 321 Out — Start from Where You Actually Are
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — the Lord Jesus said to Nathanael, "you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man." The way he read this dream was to point at that stairway and say: it is me. Brothers and sisters, here is my role model: he himself became the join between heaven and earth. And 1 Timothy 2:5 says, "there is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus."

The Bible is my standard — this chapter tells us one thing: God's promise comes before the human response. God finishes speaking in verses 13 to 15; Jacob does not open his mouth until verse 20. A standard is not a reward God hands over once we have performed well. It is a place God laid down first, and that we then walk into.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — verse 16: "Surely Yahweh is in this place, and I didn't know it." Guidance is sometimes not a new instruction at all; it is being shown something that was there the whole time. This week you can practise one question: in this situation, where is God?

Let Jesus be King — God said "I will" four times, and Jacob answered with one "if." And God caught that "if", and did not leave him standing there. Brothers and sisters, letting Jesus be King begins at the height you are actually standing at, and from there he grows you up the whole way. You do not have to wait until your prayers are mature enough before you open your mouth.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — look at how God introduces himself in verse 13: "I am Yahweh, the God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac." He does not say, "I am the God whose name you were using inside a lie an hour ago." And the first thing Jacob does when he wakes up is to name that place — he gave the name of that place to God, and not to himself.

Establish God's system — "This is none other than God's house, and this is the gate of heaven." There was no building there. There was a stone. Brothers and sisters, when we establish God's system, the decisive thing is not the premises; it is whether he is there. A church with a magnificent building and no presence of God is not Bethel. A gathering in a living room, in an office, in a hospital ward, where God is present — that is.

And here I want to say an honest word about 321 itself. We have a very clear framework for growth — the eight stages of changing our mindset, the fivefold change of mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. And this chapter reminds us that the starting point God accepts may be lower than the one we are willing to accept. Jacob's first prayer was, "if you will give me something to eat and something to wear" — and if he turned up in one of our small groups, we would probably decide his motives were impure and needed correcting. But God caught it. So when you are walking alongside a new friend, do not be in a hurry to correct the content of his prayers. Let him pray first; God will grow him up — and it is quite all right if that takes twenty years.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, the Same Stone
Brothers and sisters, the same stone under the same head falls into four different hearts, and what each one sees is different.

The proud heart says, "What a poor prayer Jacob prayed." The first thing this heart does when it finishes reading is grade other people's spiritual level. Brothers and sisters, think it over: if God decided whether or not to appear on the basis of the quality of the prayer, this chapter would not exist. And if your prayers today are more mature than Jacob's, that too is because somebody walked alongside you for a great many years.

The fearful heart says, "I am not sure God still wants me." You may have just done something very bad, and you cannot sleep. To a heart like that I want to say: look at how verse 15 ends — "For I will not leave you until I have done that which I have spoken of to you." And Hebrews 13:5 takes it up like this: "I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you." That sentence was said, the first time it was ever said, to a deceiver.

The ashamed heart says, "Somebody like me — how would I ever have heaven open over my head?" You may feel that everyone else gets visions, confirmations, a sense of God moving, and you get nothing at all. Brothers and sisters, notice this: when Jacob received that vision he was doing nothing whatever — he was asleep. The greatest grace in the whole chapter happened while he had no idea it was happening. You do not have to become spiritual first before heaven will open.

The wounded heart says, "I am on the road running away, right now, this minute." You may be in the middle of leaving somewhere — a marriage that has broken, a job you were forced to give up, a home you cannot go back to. Brothers and sisters, this chapter is for you. That night he had nothing at all but a stone. And that stone later became a pillar, and that place later became Bethel. God very often sets up, on the most wretched night of a person's life, a marker that person will keep coming back to for the next thirty years.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, pray tonight, without tidying yourself up first. Open your mouth as you are, in the mood you are actually in, with the problems you actually have. God appeared on the least deserving night of Jacob's life.

Second, ask one question: in this situation, where is God? Pick one thing that is worrying you at the moment, be quiet for three minutes, and ask only that. What usually changes is not the circumstance. It is what you are able to see.

Third, set up a pillar. Take one thing God has done in your life and record it in a way you can see — write it on the first page of a notebook, make it the wallpaper on your phone, find a stone and stand it on your desk. People forget. That is why we set up markers.

Fourth, do not look down on where somebody else is starting from. If you hear a prayer this week that sounds very "self-interested", do not correct it. Thank God for that person first — he opened his mouth.

Fifth, this week tell this lesson to one friend outside the church, in three sentences. There is a man in the Bible who deceived his own father, was hunted by his brother, ran through the night, and on the first night took a stone for a pillow. And God appeared to him on that very night, with not one word of rebuke, saying only, "I am with you, and will keep you, wherever you go." And when he woke he said one thing — "Surely Yahweh is in this place, and I didn't know it."
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that he did not come because I got better first; he came first, and that is how I slowly get better.
I declare that the road to heaven is not one I built; that stairway was let down by God, and his name is Jesus.
I declare that God has been there all along in the places where I did not know it, and I ask him to open my eyes.
I declare that I will begin at the height I am standing at now, and let him grow me up the whole way.
"Recognise him in the places that do not look as though he is there" — what does that actually look like this week?

Choose the three settings where God is least likely to cross your mind: the commute, the ten minutes at the sink, the corridor before a meeting. In those three places do the same very small thing — say one sentence, "Lord, you are here too", and then take a look at the people and the things in front of you. The point of the exercise is not to manufacture a feeling; it is to dismantle the assumption that God only turns up on certain occasions. After a week of it, write down which of the three settings moved you most; that is usually the place God wants you paying attention to. And you can add one more thing to it: give that place a name, the way Jacob called his place Bethel.
Brothers and sisters, if only one sentence from this lesson may remain, let it be verse 16:
"Surely Yahweh is in this place, and I didn't know it!"

Picture that night. A man in his thirties, away from home for the first time, walking on until the light was gone, dropping down on open ground, taking a stone for a pillow. All he had in his hand was a staff — as he says himself in Genesis 32:10, "with just my staff I crossed over this Jordan."
His mind was probably turning it over and over: will my brother come after me? Will my father hate me for the rest of his life? Will I ever be able to go back?

And it was while he had no idea it was happening that heaven opened. A stairway set upon the earth, its top reaching to heaven, the angels of God ascending and descending on it, and Yahweh standing above it, saying: I am with you.
Brothers and sisters, he did nothing at all that night. He did not pray, he did not confess, he made no resolutions. He was simply too tired to stay awake.
This is what grace looks like.

And hold on to this comparison. In chapter 11, human beings threw everything they had into building a tower to reach heaven; the building stopped, and the name was rewritten as "confusion." In chapter 28, a man on the run lay down on the ground and fell asleep; God let down a stairway, and that place was called "God's house."
People build upwards, and it does not stand. God lets down from above, and it stands.
And that stairway was later given a name. The Lord Jesus said to Nathanael, "you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man."

The focus is not on how much I have got wrong, not on whether my prayers are mature, and not on where I happen to be sleeping tonight. The focus is on Jesus — he is the stairway set upon the earth whose top reaches to heaven. Not I, but Christ.
May God bless every one of us: to pray this week just as we are, and to set up one pillar in memory of him. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ God appeared on the first night of his flight, with not one word of rebuke. How does that correct our picture of when God is willing to turn up?
2. ★★ The tower of Babel was built by people from the bottom upwards; the stairway was let down by God from the top downwards. What is that contrast saying?
3. ★ "Surely Yahweh is in this place, and I didn't know it." Which settings do we most often tie God down to?
4. ★★ Jacob's response was, "If God will be with me … then I will …" God did not rebuke him for it. What does that say to a faith that is still very self-interested?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (my own faith is the more mature one), fearful (running like this, will God still bother with me?), ashamed (I got myself into this state), wounded (somebody once told me God would never be in a place like this). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "Behold, I am with you, and will keep you, wherever you go." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Has there been a "night with a stone for a pillow" in your own life? Looking back on it now — where was God that night?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The place I least expect God to be is …"
9. ★★ This week, in which three settings will you say, "Lord, you are here too"? Name those three places out loud.

Leader's reminder: question nine will touch the low places of a life. If someone speaks about the despair of that time, stay with him first; do not rush in with "God had it all arranged." If thoughts of self-harm are involved, be sure to follow up with him privately after the meeting and help him find professional support.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own home, is there someone living through his "first night on the run"? How will you be with him this week without rebuking him first?
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or at school, who is lying there alone with a stone under his head?
12. ★★★ The practice of recognising his presence: this week, in three settings that least feel as though God is in them, say once in each, "Lord, you are here too." Say which one you will begin with.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — and tell him about your own "night with a stone for a pillow." Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First, there is a young man in the Bible who had just finished deceiving somebody and was running for his life, and who fell asleep one night with a stone under his head. Second, he dreamed of a stairway let down from heaven, and God said to him, "I am with you" — with not one word of rebuke. Third, and so I believe in a God who does not wait for people to be clean before he shows up. Write down now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the three places where you will say "Lord, you are here too" this week, and the person you are going to go and be with. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to let us recognise him in the places that least look as though he is there.
